chunks.text: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.

diagram.label: Timed-release and coated designs expect a long intestine; a shorter gut gives them less time

chunks.text: When a medicine may be poorly absorbed after resection, the care team may consider liquid, dissolvable, topical, or non-oral forms of the same drug instead.
For drugs with a narrow therapeutic range, clinicians may check drug blood levels or watch the clinical effect closely, because absorption after resection is hard to predict.
Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

diagram.label: Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel

chunks.text: Short bowel syndrome is described in three anatomy groups: end-jejunostomy (no colon), jejuno-colic (small bowel joined to part of the colon), and jejuno-ileo-colic (some ileum kept, joined to the colon). Advice on fluids and diet differs between these groups.

Remaining small-bowel length bands (for example under 100 cm with an end-jejunostomy) describe risk of needing nutrition or fluid support; they are risk bands, not a line above which everything is safe.
Hypertonic, sugary drinks such as fruit juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output or diarrhea in short bowel syndrome; they are best limited regardless of anatomy.

diagram.label: Fluid and salt balance is set in the small bowel

chunks.text: A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink to replace fluid and sodium losses in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.

diagram.label: Salt and glucose together help the small bowel absorb water

chunks.text: Fluids are generally sipped through the day rather than taken in large amounts at once, and many teams suggest separating drinks from meals.
People with short bowel syndrome are usually encouraged to eat about six small meals or snacks a day rather than three large meals.
The goal is to eat more than before surgery to make up for losses (compensatory hyperphagia), not to restrict intake; amounts are set individually by the care team.
When the colon is in continuity, complex carbohydrates can be partly salvaged by colonic bacteria, so a diet richer in complex carbohydrates is usually favored for this group.

diagram.label: A colon can recover some energy from starches

chunks.text: With the colon in continuity, fat malabsorption raises oxalate absorption and kidney stone risk; many teams advise limiting high-oxalate foods for this group.
Concentrated simple sugars (sweets, syrups, sweetened drinks) draw water into the bowel and are generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
Antimotility medicines (for example loperamide) are a mainstay to slow transit and reduce output; timing relative to meals is set by the care team.
Gastric acid hypersecretion is common early after major resection, and acid-suppressing medicines are often used to reduce output; their release form still matters for absorption.
Thirst, dark or reduced urine, dizziness on standing, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration that should be raised with the care team promptly.
Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.

diagram.label: This design needs time in a gut that is now shorter

chunks.text: Extended-release products are generally avoided after extensive resection; an immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often a question worth asking the pharmacist about.
Enteric-coated and delayed-release products are designed to pass the stomach before dissolving; with rapid transit, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some pass through intact.
Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.

For plain immediate-release tablets only, crushing or dissolving may improve absorption in some patients; this is a decision for the pharmacist. Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated products defeats their design and can be dangerous.

Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, draw water into the gut, and can raise stoma output or diarrhea; they are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines and sugar-free products.
If a medicine does not seem to produce its expected effect, malabsorption should be suspected and raised with the prescriber or pharmacist.
A pharmacist review of every medicine's form and inactive ingredients is recommended after major bowel resection.

With an end-jejunostomy, plain water, tea, coffee and other low-sodium (hypotonic) drinks can pull sodium into the gut and increase output, so these drinks are usually limited in favor of an oral rehydration solution.

diagram.label: Without a colon, the remaining jejunum sets your fluid balance

chunks.text: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.

diagram.label: A colon absorbs much of the water and salt

chunks.text: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.
Typical sports drinks are low in sodium and high in sugar compared with an SBS oral rehydration solution, so they are not a substitute for it.
Salting food and choosing salty snacks is commonly encouraged in short bowel syndrome with high output, within the care team's advice for the person's heart and kidney health.
Starchy, low-fiber foods such as white rice, bananas, potatoes, pasta and plain crackers are often reported to thicken output.

Fat restriction is mainly useful when the colon is in continuity (because of oxalate and fatty-acid effects in the colon); with an end-jejunostomy, fat is an important energy source and is usually not restricted.
Lactose does not need to be removed for most people with short bowel syndrome; small portions of dairy, especially cheese and yogurt, are often tolerated.
Caffeine and alcohol can increase output and fluid losses and are usually limited in short bowel syndrome.

Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).

An intact tablet or shell seen in the pouch can mean the medicine did not dissolve, or it can be an empty shell left after the drug was released. It is worth showing the pharmacist; it is not proof either way.
In the pilot study, 11 of 50 interviewed ostomy patients had seen undissolved medicine, and over 60% said they had not been told how an ostomy can affect their medicines.

With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually intact and oral medicines are often absorbed normally; but the stoma type alone does not tell you remaining small-bowel length, so it is not a guarantee.
How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.
The large intestine matters mainly for slow-release products, which may release part of their dose there; without a colon, those products have less time and surface to release.

diagram.label: Slow-release products can rely on the colon for part of their release

chunks.text: Patients should consult a pharmacist before changing the dose form of a medicine, such as crushing, splitting or switching products.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.

Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.
Because the change in absorption differs from drug to drug, each medicine should be considered individually with the prescriber or pharmacist.

WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (2003) contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.
Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.

diagram.label: Glucose and sodium carry water in together in the small bowel
